solver_candidate_counterexample: Take b=3 and e_1=1, e_2=1, e_3=6. Then for the hypothesis: for d=1, the left side is 3 and the right side is 3; for d=2, the left side is 1 (only 6 is divisible by 2) and the right side is 1 (only 2 is divisible by 2); for d=3, the left side is 1 (only 6 is divisible by 3) and the right side is 1 (only 3 is divisible by 3); for every d>=4, the right side is 0 since no element of {1,2,3} is divisible by d, so the inequality is automatic. Hence the stated hypothesis is satisfied. But in S=Q[y_1,y_2,y_3] with deg(y_1)=1, deg(y_2)=2, deg(y_3)=3, every homogeneous polynomial of degree 1 is a scalar multiple of y_1. So any two homogeneous degree-1 elements u_1,u_2 are linearly dependent; in particular, if u_1 is nonzero then u_2 lies in the ideal (u_1), so the image of u_2 in S/(u_1) is 0. Therefore u_2 cannot be a non-zero-divisor modulo (u_1), and the ordered list u_1,u_2,u_3 cannot be a regular sequence. Thus the lemma statement is false as written.
solver_summary: A concrete counterexample is b=3 with (e_1,e_2,e_3)=(1,1,6). The divisibility-count hypothesis holds for every positive integer d, but no regular sequence of homogeneous elements of degrees 1,1,6 can exist in S=Q[y_1,y_2,y_3] with deg(y_1)=1, deg(y_2)=2, deg(y_3)=3, because the degree-1 homogeneous subspace of S is one-dimensional, spanned by y_1.
